evaluated.name: OperatingCoverageOfObligations
evaluated.hypothesis: Profitability scaled by the actual stock of obligations it must cover (rather than by assets) is the economically correct distress-adjusted profitability measure and predicts returns beyond either operating margin or leverage separately.
evaluated.reasoning: The numerator is operating income after the cash cost of debt, and the denominator is long-term plus current claims, so the ratio is a direct coverage/solvency-runway metric that mechanically fuses both themes. Firms with high coverage are misclassified as risky by leverage-based screens and earn a premium relative to their perceived default probability; winsorization limits the influence of tiny-denominator outliers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DeficitFirmProfitabilityScreen
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms with accumulated deficits (negative retained earnings, an Altman-style distress marker), current operating profitability separates genuine recoveries from value traps, while for healthy firms it carries less incremental information.
evaluated.reasoning: The indicator switches the profitability signal on only inside the distressed subpopulation, so the long-short spread is a within-distress profitability sort rather than a market-wide profitability sort. Deficit firms are shunned and cheaply priced, so those already earning operating income are the most mispriced, while deficit firms with operating losses face real dilution and default risk.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetDebtWeightedOperatingProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oiadp, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Operating profitability is priced correctly for cash-rich, debt-free firms but is badly underpriced for firms carrying substantial net debt, because investors apply a blanket distress discount to levered equity without conditioning on whether operations comfortably service that debt.
evaluated.reasoning: The weight is a non-negative cross-sectional rank of net debt (debt minus cash) to assets in [0,1], so the signal is monotone increasing in industry-demeaned operating profitability everywhere and simply loses intensity as the balance sheet becomes clean — a firm with no net debt is scored near zero rather than being pushed into the long or short leg. This removes the sign ambiguity of the demeaned product: the long leg is unambiguously profitable-and-levered firms and the short leg is unprofitable-and-levered firms, exactly the offset mechanism. Using oiadp net of depreciation and industry z-scoring, with a net-debt (not gross-leverage) conditioner, separates it from a raw gross-profitability restatement.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LeveredTurnaroundTrend
evaluated.hypothesis: A persistent improvement in operating profitability raises equity value convexly for a levered firm, because equity is a residual claim whose value rises sharply as default probability falls; the same profitability trend is nearly irrelevant for an unlevered firm.
evaluated.reasoning: The leverage leg is now a non-negative [0,1] rank, so deteriorating profitability at a low-leverage firm scores near zero instead of strongly positive, and the score is monotone in the profitability trend with intensity proportional to the equity-holder payoff elasticity. The short leg becomes levered firms with sustained profitability deterioration — the population where default probability is actively rising — while the long leg is levered firms visibly repairing coverage; a four-period TREND enforces persistence without the coverage cost of a longer window.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashFlowVolatilityLeverageDefaultProxy
evaluated.hypothesis: Default risk is driven by the joint occurrence of unstable operating profitability and heavy debt, in the Merton distance-to-default sense; levered firms whose operating profitability is stable are far safer than their leverage ratio suggests and are underpriced by investors who screen on leverage alone.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the multi-leg quality-composite construction entirely and instead uses a second-moment property of profitability that only becomes economically dangerous when scaled by a non-negative debt-intensity rank, so unlevered firms with volatile earnings are neutral rather than shorted. The long leg is stable-profit levered firms (mispriced as distressed) and the short leg is volatile-profit levered firms (genuinely close to the default boundary), which is an interaction with no single-theme analogue since neither profit volatility nor leverage alone identifies this state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EbitdaPlusCashRunway
evaluated.hypothesis: What determines near-term survival is whether one year of operating cash generation plus the existing cash stock covers the claims coming due within the year; firms with a long runway are misclassified as risky by leverage screens and are underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the accepted coverage ratio's two weaknesses — it drops `xint` (the main cause of its 0.119 coverage) and replaces the long-dated debt denominator, which collapses for near-debt-free firms, with current liabilities, which are strictly positive for essentially all operating firms. The numerator fuses profitability (oibdp) with the liquidity buffer (che), so the ratio is a genuine cross-theme survival horizon rather than either an EBITDA margin or a current ratio.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EarningsDistanceToDefault
evaluated.hypothesis: Default proximity is the ratio of the earnings cushion over total liabilities to the volatility of that earnings stream; firms with high and stable coverage are far safer than their raw leverage implies and earn abnormal returns relative to the risk investors assign them.
evaluated.reasoning: Gen-0's volatility-times-leverage construction pointed the right way (alpha +1.8%, t=1.55) but multiplied a second moment by a weight without any level of profitability, discarding the numerator of the distance-to-default concept; combining the coverage level with earnings stability restores the mean/volatility structure. Rank aggregation is essential here because oiadp/lt is extremely fat-tailed for low-liability firms, and the two legs are economically complementary rather than redundant (level of cushion vs. reliability of cushion).
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ChronicOperatingLossesWithDebt
evaluated.hypothesis: A single loss year is noise, but a firm that has posted operating losses in most of the last five years while carrying meaningful debt is in a self-reinforcing distress spiral, and investors persistently over-extrapolate the possibility of a turnaround in exactly this group.
evaluated.reasoning: The persistence count captures a state — chronic inability to cover operating costs — that levels, trends, and volatility all miss, and multiplying by a non-negative debt-intensity rank means chronically lossmaking but debt-free firms (which can simply shrink) score near zero rather than being shorted. The short leg is therefore narrow and economically specific: repeated operating losses financed by creditors, the classic lottery-like distressed equity that underperforms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkProfitSolvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Profitability and solvency are complements, not substitutes: a firm is genuinely safe only if it ranks well on both, and strength on one dimension cannot compensate for weakness on the other, so the binding constraint — the minimum of the two ranks — should price better than any additive composite.
evaluated.reasoning: Additive composites (SUMRANK, sums of z-scores) let a spectacular profit margin mask a leveraged balance sheet, which gen-0 evidence suggests is precisely the value-trap configuration that destroys FF5 alpha; MIN removes that offsetting by construction and places only jointly strong firms in the long leg. Pairing this with SIGNAL 1 and SIGNAL 4 makes the batch informative about functional form itself — multiplicative gating versus rank addition versus complementarity — while holding the underlying profitability and net-debt content roughly fixed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashConversionUnderMaturityPressure
evaluated.hypothesis: Reported operating profit that fails to convert into operating cash flow is only dangerous when obligations are imminent; firms whose EBITDA is trapped in working capital while a large slice of debt matures within twelve months face a funding shortfall the market recognizes late.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the level-of-profitability gate that made the previous version an affine transform of an archived signal and instead uses the profitability *conversion gap* (oibdp minus oancf) — a quality dimension untested in the archive — gated by debt maturity structure rather than leverage level, a distinct distress channel from the net-debt and total-liability ranks already evaluated. The weight is a non-negative [0,1] rank of short-term debt to assets, so cash-converting firms with no near-term maturities sit near zero rather than being forced into either leg, and the short leg is the economically specific group whose paper profits must be refinanced.
REASONING_NOTE: not applicable

evaluated.name: DistressFinancingWithoutProfits
evaluated.hypothesis: New borrowing is not informative on its own — it funds investment at profitable firms and funds losses at weak ones; debt raised by firms with poor operating profitability is distress financing and predicts underperformance, while debt repayment by weak firms signals genuine repair.
evaluated.reasoning:
The revision replaces the incommensurate raw-unit difference with a true conditional structure: a standardized debt-issuance measure multiplied by a non-negative [0,1] rank of *un*profitability, so a highly profitable firm issuing debt receives a near-zero score instead of being shorted, which is exactly the restriction the unconditional external-financing anomaly does not impose. The signal therefore cannot be reproduced by RMW plus a debt-issuance factor in a linear combination, and its tails are populated only by weak-profitability firms whose financing direction differs, making the long-short spread a clean test of the interaction.
REASONING_NOTE: not applicable
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LeveredMarginCompression
evaluated.hypothesis: Financially stretched firms defend liquidity by cutting prices and dumping inventory, so a falling gross margin at a levered firm is the product-market footprint of an unfolding distress spiral, while margin expansion under leverage signals pricing power that de-risks the debt.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's turnaround attempt used a multi-year trend in oiadp/at — an aggregate that mixes margin, turnover, and depreciation policy — whereas gross margin change isolates the product-market channel through which distress actually propagates, and a one-year change avoids the coverage cost of a four-period trend. The non-negative leverage rank ensures margin swings at debt-free firms score near zero, so the spread contrasts levered firms whose pricing power is improving against levered firms discounting to raise cash.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MaintenanceAndDebtCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm's true fixed claims are debt service *plus* the capital consumption it must replace to stay in business; EBITDA measured against this combined burden is a better solvency-adjusted profitability measure than EBITDA over debt alone.
evaluated.reasoning: This directly repairs the denominator-collapse flaw the critic identified in OperatingCoverageOfObligations (which still delivered the archive's best FMB slope of 2.29): depreciation is strictly positive for essentially every operating firm, so the denominator never vanishes for low-debt firms and winsorization is no longer doing the heavy lifting. Economically it makes capital-intensive levered firms — which need cash for both lenders and asset replacement — score low even when EBITDA margins look healthy, a distinction no debt-only coverage ratio makes.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CoverageWithinOwnHistory
evaluated.hypothesis: Credit quality is judged by investors in cross-sectional levels, so they are slow to recognize when a firm's own debt-service capacity has moved to the top of its five-year range; within-firm improvement in EBITDA per dollar of liabilities is credit repair that has not yet been repriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the MIN-combiner family entirely and tests an orthogonal question — position of the profitability-to-obligations ratio inside its own history rather than its cross-sectional level — which no archived signal addresses, so it is nearly uncorrelated with the 3.56-t WeakestLink result by construction. Self-normalization also solves the fat-tail problem that gave the runway ratio a 0.35 FMB slope, since TS_RANK is bounded in [0,1] for every firm regardless of liability scale, and using lt rather than debt avoids zero denominators.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TotalLeverageSqueeze
evaluated.hypothesis: Operating leverage and financial leverage compound: a firm whose cost structure is dominated by fixed overhead and capital consumption converts a modest revenue shortfall into an EBITDA collapse, and if that firm is also levered the shortfall lands directly on the debt service, so total leverage — not financial leverage alone — determines distress exposure.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the flagged same-denominator rank decomposition with a genuinely different distress dimension — the fixed-versus-variable composition of the cost base, which no archived signal measures — interacted with balance-sheet leverage, so it cannot be reproduced by cash-holdings or EBITDA-coverage variables. The non-negative leverage rank keeps high-fixed-cost but unlevered firms near zero, isolating the compounded-leverage tail as the short leg while low-fixed-cost levered firms (flexible, able to shrink costs with revenue) form the long leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FundingStabilityAmplifiedProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress risk depends on when obligations come due, not only on how large they are; a profitable firm funded with long-dated debt can capitalize its earnings power, whereas the same profitability at a firm whose claims are all current is consumed by rollover risk and creditor bargaining.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the working-capital accrual term the critic identified as Sloan in disguise and instead conditions profitability on the maturity *composition* of the liability side — a distress dimension untested in the archive, which has only used leverage levels, net cash, and dlc/assets. The weight is bounded in [0,1] with an essentially always-positive denominator, so the signal stays monotone in profitability while concentrating intensity in firms whose funding structure lets earnings accrue to equity rather than to imminent creditors.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AfterTaxProfitToLiabilities
evaluated.hypothesis: Taxes are a senior cash claim that must be settled before creditors or shareholders, so the correct measure of debt-service capacity is operating profit after depreciation and after tax, relative to the full stock of liabilities; firms whose post-tax operating profit genuinely covers their obligations are safer than leverage screens imply.
evaluated.reasoning: The revision fixes both defects the critic identified: tax expense is now matched against a post-depreciation profit measure rather than EBITDA, so the construct is a cash-claim coverage ratio rather than a capital-intensity proxy, and it is no longer a book-tax difference restatement because taxes enter as a deduction from distributable profit instead of as a separate ranked leg. Total liabilities in the denominator are strictly positive for operating firms, so unlike EBITDA-over-debt the ratio does not explode for near-debt-free firms, and winsorization handles only the residual tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SolvencyLiquidityWeakestLink
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency and liquidity are distinct failure modes — a firm dies either because earnings cannot service structural claims or because cash cannot meet claims due this year — and equity is only genuinely safe when neither constraint binds, so the weaker of the two coverages should price.
evaluated.reasoning: This joins the archive's best cross-sectional construct (fixed-claim coverage, FMB 2.74) with the cash-liquidity dimension that drove the runway's 4.3-t alpha, but unlike the flagged runway decomposition the two legs have different numerators *and* different denominators, so neither leg can dominate the other mechanically. The MIN combiner is the one functional form that has produced both a significant slope and a significant alpha in this archive, and applying it to solvency-versus-liquidity rather than profitability-versus-net-cash makes it economically distinct from WeakestLinkProfitSolvency.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: StressTestedFixedClaimCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for default is not average debt-service capacity but capacity in the firm's bad states; a company whose *worst* coverage over five years still cleared its fixed claims has demonstrated it can survive its own downturn, and this demonstrated resilience is not priced by level-based leverage screens.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's second-moment attempt (VOL of ROA times leverage) only measured dispersion and ignored the level of the cushion, while CoverageWithinOwnHistory measured relative position and discarded the level entirely — TS_MIN keeps the economically relevant object, the realized floor of the coverage ratio, which is the direct empirical analogue of a stress test. It is a genuinely different temporal concept from levels, trends, and volatility, and because it is applied to a ratio with a strictly positive denominator it inherits the robustness that made the fixed-claim coverage family the archive's best-slope signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AssetBackingSubstitutesForProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings power and liquid asset backing are *substitutes* for survival — a weakly profitable firm whose current assets already cover its liabilities is not distressed, and a firm with thin asset backing is safe if it earns enough — so the relevant state is the stronger of the two protections, not the weaker.
evaluated.reasoning: Every combiner tested so far assumes complementarity (MIN) or multiplicative gating; MAX tests the opposite economic claim, and pairing it with a liquidation-coverage leg (current assets over total liabilities) that appears nowhere in the archive means a positive result would identify a genuinely different survival channel rather than restating the MIN winner. Comparing this against SIGNAL 1 and the archived MIN signal will tell us whether the profitability-distress interaction is one of joint requirement or of mutual insurance, which is the central unresolved question of this theme pair.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RepaymentHorizonDeterioration
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically informative quantity is not the level of obligations relative to earning power but the direction in which the repayment horizon is moving; a firm whose liabilities per dollar of gross profit lengthened over the past year is migrating toward distress regardless of where its leverage level currently sits.
evaluated.reasoning: This leaves the saturated level-coverage family entirely and measures the one-year change in the years-of-gross-profit-to-repay statistic, which moves when either obligations grow or the profit base erodes — a deterioration state that no level ratio, and no separate debt-issuance or profitability anomaly, can express because it requires both themes inside a single time difference. Gross profit is used as the deflator because it is the cut-proof earnings layer, and both inputs are near-universally reported, so coverage stays at the archive's high end while the differencing removes the persistent industry and capital-structure level effects that make level ratios correlate with published anomalies.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LeverageAccretionSpread
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt destroys equity value exactly when the return earned on assets falls below the rate actually paid on liabilities; the sign and size of this spread — not leverage or profitability separately — determines whether borrowing is accretive or is quietly transferring value from shareholders to creditors.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a mechanism the archive has never tested: it uses the firm's *realized* borrowing cost, which is the price lenders charge for its credit risk, and compares it to the operating return that must fund it, so the same numerical leverage means something different for a firm borrowing at 4% than at 14%. Deflating interest by total liabilities rather than by debt keeps the denominator away from zero for lightly indebted firms, and the spread is a difference of two bounded rates rather than a fat-tailed coverage multiple, which should support a coherent cross-sectional slope as well as a portfolio spread.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueScaledRefinancingGap
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency should be judged against business scale rather than against the balance sheet: the cents of operating profit left per revenue dollar after covering the debt maturing this year measure how large a firm's near-term financing hole is relative to the ongoing operations that must plug it.
evaluated.reasoning: Every coverage construct in the archive is denominated in assets or liabilities, so their cross-sectional variation is dominated by capital intensity and book leverage; revenue is a stable, strictly positive, non-accounting-discretionary scale variable, which makes this a different statistical object rather than another numerator swap in the same family. Subtracting current debt from EBITDA inside the numerator creates a genuine profitability-distress interaction — a high-margin firm with a maturity wall and a thin-margin firm with none can score identically — and the always-positive denominator avoids the degeneracy that forced heavy winsorization elsewhere.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SolvencyWithWorkingCapitalSlack
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(wcap, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The liquidity half of the survival condition is not about cash hoards specifically but about the whole stock of self-liquidating resources — receivables and inventory net of current claims — that can be converted before creditors force the issue.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic's standing objection to the leader is that its liquidity leg is the published cash-holdings anomaly; replacing cash-over-current-liabilities with working capital over total liabilities keeps the economic role identical while removing the cash-holdings content, so a comparable result attributes the leader's power to near-term solvency rather than to cash levels, and a materially weaker result attributes it to cash. Working capital is reported for essentially all operating firms, so this attribution test comes at no coverage cost.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SolvencyLiquidityMismatch
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms fail from illiquidity, not from insolvency on paper; a company whose earnings comfortably cover structural claims but whose cash cannot meet this year's claims is exactly the case where the market prices the visible income statement and underweights the binding funding constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than adding a leg to the archive's MIN construct, this asks the opposite and previously untested question — what does the *gap* between the two protections predict — which is the sharpest possible statement of the theme's premise that profitability is mispriced differently near distress. The two legs are the same objects whose joint minimum won, so a significant negative slope here identifies that the winner's power comes from the liquidity constraint binding on apparently profitable firms rather than from a generic quality composite, and the sign is unambiguous because the measure is a difference of two bounded ranks.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FreeCashMarginAfterSeniorClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: What is left for shareholders is operating profit after every senior claim has been paid — capital replacement, lenders, and the tax authority — and expressing that residual per dollar of revenue measures how much cushion the business model provides before the equity claim goes to zero.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a smoothing robustness check with a complete accounting of the seniority stack in a single expression, something no archived signal attempts: existing coverage ratios net out at most one senior claim and scale by balance-sheet stocks, whereas this nets all three and scales by revenue, a strictly positive, non-discretionary measure of business scale. The revenue-scaled family has produced portfolio alpha (RevenueScaledRefinancingGap, 2.5%/t 2.46) with an incomplete numerator, so completing the claim stack is a substantive economic change rather than a re-weighting of published legs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CoverageLevelAndDirection
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is credibly out of danger only when its fixed-claim coverage is both high and improving; high-but-deteriorating and low-but-recovering coverage are ambiguous states that the market treats as if only the current level mattered.
evaluated.reasoning: The state-versus-direction complementarity is retained because it is a genuinely new combiner for this archive, but the burden ratio is inverted so that the denominator (depreciation plus debt) is strictly positive for every operating firm, which removes the sign-flip that let negative-gross-profit firms masquerade as low-burden in the flagged version. Both legs are now monotone in the same economic direction, so the long leg is unambiguously firms with strong and strengthening debt-service capacity and the short leg is weak and weakening firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CreditRepricingShock
evaluated.hypothesis: Lenders reprice a deteriorating borrower before accountants or equity investors do, so a jump in the interest actually paid per dollar of liabilities is a credit-quality downgrade revealed through the income statement, and it predicts equity underperformance as the higher funding cost compounds into future profitability.
evaluated.reasoning: The flagged version was dominated by the change in ROA — an established earnings-momentum predictor — so the operating-return term is removed entirely and only the lender-set price of credit remains, an information source no archived signal uses. Deflating interest expense by total liabilities rather than by debt keeps the denominator away from zero for lightly indebted firms, and differencing removes the persistent cross-sectional variation in capital structure and coupon vintage, isolating the year-over-year repricing event.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FixedChargeAbsorptionYears
evaluated.hypothesis: The right unit for measuring a solvency buffer is time, not a ratio to assets: net worth divided by the firm's annual unavoidable charges says how many years of capital consumption and interest the equity cushion can absorb before the balance sheet is exhausted.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the unweighted sum of published legs and introduces a denominator concept absent from the archive — the firm's own recurring fixed charges — which converts a static leverage stock into a survival horizon and therefore means something different for a capital-light service firm than for a leveraged manufacturer with the same book leverage. Depreciation is strictly positive for operating firms, so the denominator never vanishes, and the measure is naturally comparable across the cross-section because it is denominated in years rather than in accounting units.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: JointStressFloorResilience
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 5)), RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(wcap, lt), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm has demonstrated survivability only if it stayed solvent *and* liquid through its own worst year of the past five; the joint historical floor of the two constraints measures proven resilience, whereas a contemporaneous snapshot rewards firms that are merely enjoying a good year.
evaluated.reasoning: The downside-floor statistic and the complementarity combiner are the two highest-Sharpe ideas in the archive (0.199 and 0.222) but have never been used together, and their combination is a distinct economic object — a realized two-dimensional stress test rather than a smoothing of either leg. It also directly addresses the standing worry about the floor concept: if the joint floor beats the joint level, resilience through bad states is priced beyond the current state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LifetimeCushionAndCoverage
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(re, lt)), RANK(RATIO(oibdp, ADD(dp, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The second condition for safety may not be near-term liquidity at all but accumulated self-financing history: a firm whose lifetime retained profits are large relative to its obligations has demonstrated that its claims were funded by earnings rather than by creditors, and current coverage tells us whether that remains true.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the decisive attribution test left on the leading recipe — the same combiner and the same coverage leg, but the second leg replaced by a slow-moving accumulated-profit cushion instead of a liquid-resource stock, so a comparable result means the interaction is about self-funding history while a weaker result confirms it is genuinely about near-term liquidity. Retained earnings are essentially unused in the archive (the only prior attempt was a degenerate indicator gate), and re/lt is economically distinct from both cash and working capital because it is a cumulative flow, not a stock of assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PooledResourceCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Creditors are repaid from whatever is available — a year of operating earnings or the liquidation of net working capital — so the economically correct measure pools both resources against the pooled claim stock of maturing debt and unavoidable capital replacement.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN winners assert the two resource types are non-substitutable, and this tests the opposite in dollar space rather than rank space, which matters because dollar pooling weights each firm's actual magnitudes instead of its cross-sectional position — the design feature shared by the archive's best cross-sectional slopes (MaintenanceAndDebtCoverage 2.74, AfterTaxProfitToLiabilities 2.03). The denominator includes depreciation and is therefore strictly positive, so unlike EBITDA-over-debt it does not degenerate for lightly indebted firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DualLiquidityCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Near-term claim coverage is the priced dimension of distress, and it is measured with error by any single accounting cut; averaging a stock-based measure (net working capital against all claims) with a flow-plus-cash measure (earnings and cash against current claims) isolates the common signal and diversifies the noise.
evaluated.reasoning: The mismatch result implies the liquidity dimension, not the structural-coverage dimension, is what generates FF5 alpha in this theme pair, so the natural next step is to measure that dimension twice and average, which is a different exercise from combining liquidity with solvency and should sharpen the alpha t-statistic if measurement error rather than economics limited the earlier constructs. Both legs are near-universally reported and each contains a profitability component or a claims deflator, keeping the construct cross-theme while avoiding the fat-tailed raw-ratio scaling that flattened earlier slopes.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitableButIlliquid
evaluated.hypothesis: Profitability does not protect a firm that cannot fund its claims: firms that are visibly profitable *and* short of net working capital relative to their obligations are the cell where investors extrapolate the income statement and underweight the funding constraint, so this specific combination should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: The archived mismatch signal delivered the largest alpha t-statistic in the archive (−5.25) but almost no cross-sectional slope (1.02), because a linear rank difference is dominated by the liquidity leg and pools the profitable-illiquid cell with the unprofitable-liquid cell; MIN instead requires both conditions to hold, so the short leg contains only firms that are simultaneously high-margin and liquidity-poor. This is the sharpest available statement of the theme's premise — that operating profitability is priced differently depending on distress proximity — and it changes the identified population rather than relabeling an operator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginAndObligationLoadPerSale
evaluated.hypothesis: Credit analysts judge survivability in unit-economics terms: each sales dollar must carry both a healthy production margin and a light load of accumulated obligations, and a firm failing either test is fragile regardless of how its balance-sheet ratios look.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the post-hoc sign reversal with the standard prior — obligations that are large relative to the revenue base and margins that are thin both raise default risk — and it works entirely in the per-revenue normalization family, which the archive has touched only once (RevenueScaledRefinancingGap, alpha t 2.46) and never in complementarity form. Both legs are strictly-positive-denominator quantities, so ranks are monotone in the intended economic direction with no sign-flip contamination, and revenue and COGS are near-universally reported so coverage stays at the archive's high end.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginAndLiquidityWeakestLink
evaluated.hypothesis: The two priced dimensions of this theme pair are unit-economics profitability and the adequacy of liquid resources against claims; pairing the strongest slope-generating leg with the strongest alpha-generating leg should dominate either pairing tested so far.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows gross margin per sales drives the FMB slope (3.34 in MarginAndObligationLoadPerSale) while working-capital-over-liabilities drives portfolio alpha (4.9% in SolvencyWithWorkingCapitalSlack), but the two have never been combined — every prior pairing used either two claim-load legs or two liquidity legs. The legs are economically independent (an income-statement efficiency measure and a balance-sheet adequacy measure) and share no variable, so this is a genuine cross-family test rather than a re-parameterization.

evaluated.name: NetObligationLoadPerSale

considered.hypothesis: A creditor's real question is how many dollars of durable profit the firm generates even in its worst recent year for every dollar of obligation outstanding; measured in dollars rather than as a ratio of ratios, this is a direct stress-tested repayment capacity.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the flagged smoothing swap, this changes the object rather than the operator: the numerator is the firm's trough *dollar* gross profit and the denominator is the claim stack, so scale enters economically instead of being normalized away in both legs as it is in every per-sales construct tested so far. Orientation is internally consistent — a firm with a loss-making trough gets a negative numerator and lands correctly at the bottom — and total liabilities are strictly positive so the ratio never degenerates.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MaturityConcentrationWithMargin
considered.hypothesis: What forces default is timing, not size: a firm with healthy unit economics whose obligations are spread over many years cannot be pushed into insolvency, whereas the same claim stack bunched into the next twelve months creates a rollover event the market prices late.
considered.reasoning: Every load leg in the archive measures the *size* of claims relative to some scale variable, so the share of claims falling due within a year is genuinely new information — a dimensionless timing measure that is uncorrelated with the level of leverage by construction. The archive's only prior maturity-structure attempt (dltt share of long-term plus current claims) was crippled by the multiplicative z-score gate that failed across the board, so the mechanism itself has never had a fair test in the combiner that works here.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashMarginAndClaimLoad
considered.hypothesis: Obligations are settled in cash, not in accrual profit, so the margin leg that matters is operating cash flow per sales dollar; if the archive's alpha comes from genuine cash generation rather than from reported production spreads, the cash version should be at least as strong.
considered.reasoning: The alpha-generating leg of every leading signal has been an accrual margin, and cash flow from operations has never been paired with the claim-load leg, so this replaces the information content of that leg rather than its functional form — the two rank firms very differently wherever working-capital swings or non-cash charges are large. The cost is a modest coverage reduction from cash-flow-statement availability, which is acceptable for a test that identifies whether the mechanism is accounting margin or cash conversion, and which would redirect the final generation if cash wins.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IndustryRelativeMarginFloorAndLoad
considered.hypothesis: Durable competitive advantage is best measured as the firm's worst realized margin judged against its industry peers, because both the level and the cyclicality of margins are technology-determined; that peer-relative floor, paired with a light claim load, identifies firms whose obligations are safe through the cycle.
considered.reasoning: The two independently best-performing enhancements to the margin leg — industry conditioning (slope 4.05) and the five-year floor (slope 3.56, Sharpe 0.266) — address different problems (sector composition versus downside durability) and have never been applied together, so their combination is a genuine test rather than a re-parameterization. If margin floors are themselves industry-specific, this should deliver the strongest slope in the archive while retaining the leading family's alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginFloorAndMaturityTiming
considered.hypothesis: Proven downside earning power and an unconcentrated maturity schedule are the two conditions that make a claim stack harmless: the first ensures cash keeps arriving in bad states, the second ensures no creditor can demand it all at once.
considered.reasoning: This pairs the timing leg that generated the archive's best positive alpha t-statistic with the resilience-based margin leg rather than the industry-relative one, which — read against SIGNAL 2 — identifies which enhancement of the profitability leg best complements claim timing, the last open question in the family. Neither leg measures the *size* of obligations, so a strong result would establish that the profitability-distress interaction is fundamentally about durability and timing rather than about leverage levels, the most economically interesting conclusion the search could reach.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginWithClaimStructureIndex
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(lt, revt)), NEG(RATIO(dlc, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: Distress risk has one profitability dimension and one *claim-structure* dimension, and the latter is itself two-sided — how big the stack is relative to the revenue base and how much of it demands cash within the year — so the structure should be summarized as an index and then complemented against margin, not stacked as a third binding constraint.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the triple MIN with a two-level design fixes exactly the defect identified: the claim-size and claim-timing ranks are averaged rather than minimized, which preserves cross-sectional dispersion on the distress side instead of collapsing onto whichever rank is lowest and creating ties. Economically it also states the correct asymmetry — profitability and claim structure are complements (a firm needs both), whereas size and timing are partial substitutes within the same balance sheet, since a large stack that is entirely long-dated and a small stack that is entirely current can be equally survivable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginAndCashDemandingClaimShare
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(xint, dlc), lt))))
considered.hypothesis: What makes a claim stack dangerous is the fraction of it that demands cash this year — interest plus maturing principal as a share of total obligations — because that share, not the stack's size, determines whether creditors can force a liquidity event.
considered.reasoning: This is not an industry-demeaning of the archived maturity-share signal: the load leg is a new object that combines the lender-set interest rate with the maturity schedule into a single cash-demand intensity, so two firms with identical dlc/lt are now separated by the coupon their creditors charge. It keeps the alpha-generating logic of claim timing (which delivered the archive's best positive alpha t of 4.50) while adding credit-price information that no archived leg contains, at a modest coverage cost from interest expense.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NonCashWorkingCapitalMarginAndLoad
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(oibdp, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), revt)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(lt, revt))))
considered.hypothesis: The margin that services obligations is operating profit less the investment in non-cash working capital that growth in receivables and inventory absorbs; firms whose sales convert to cash rather than to operating assets can carry claims that would strangle equally profitable but cash-hungry competitors.
considered.reasoning: The critique was decisive and is fully repaired: netting the change in act minus cash minus non-debt current liabilities removes both the cash balance and short-term borrowing from the working-capital measure, so successful cash conversion no longer mechanically penalizes the firm. This preserves the economics behind the archive's highest-Sharpe result (the cash-margin pairing, 0.476) while rebuilding it from universally reported balance-sheet items instead of the cash-flow statement that limited coverage to 0.089.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: StressedCoverageAndNearTermWall
considered.hypothesis: Structural solvency and near-term liquidity are the two independent hurdles: trough-year gross profit must be large relative to the whole claim stack, and the slice of debt maturing this year must be small relative to the revenue base that has to refinance or repay it.
considered.reasoning: The redundancy objection is addressed by replacing the second gross-profit leg with a claim-timing measure that shares no numerator with the first — one leg is a stressed multi-year solvency test against total liabilities, the other a current refinancing-wall test against sales. This pairs the archive's strongest cross-sectional leg (trough gross profit over claims, slope 4.16, coverage 0.145) with the claim-timing dimension that has produced its strongest alphas, which is the combination most likely to deliver joint evidence in the closing round.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: The profitability leg is a direct restatement of Novy-Marx gross profitability, and the product of two demeaned z-scores is sign-ambiguous — it assigns equally high scores to unprofitable low-leverage firms as to profitable levered firms, which flatly contradicts the stated hypothesis and would blur the long leg.

A coherent, internally consistent coverage ratio that genuinely fuses profitability and obligation stock in one denominator, though it is close to standard credit-analysis EBITDA/debt metrics and will behave erratically for near-debt-free firms where the denominator collapses (winsorization only partially fixes this).

Beyond being an accrual-anomaly (Sloan) restatement with a leverage tilt, the double-z-score product implies that low-accrual, low-leverage firms — the safest, highest-quality cohort — receive a large positive score and are predicted to underperform, which is internally inconsistent with the stated mechanism.

The indicator gating is logically consistent with the hypothesis and delivers a genuine within-distress profitability sort rather than a market-wide one, but the ~60-70% mass at exactly zero makes the middle of the distribution meaningless and the tails entirely deficit-firm-driven, so coverage and portfolio-stability diagnostics must be scrutinized.

The convex-equity-claim mechanism is the most economically distinctive of the batch, but the construction repeats the demeaned-product flaw — deteriorating profitability at low-leverage firms scores strongly positive — so the interaction should use a non-negative leverage weight (e.g., a [0,1] rank) rather than a z-score before it is worth testing.

This is effectively a rebuild of Altman/Piotroski-style quality composites from three individually published legs (cash-based operating profitability, retained-earnings-to-assets, working-capital liquidity), and the nested SUMRANK silently double-weights the cash-profitability leg, so any result will be hard to attribute to a novel cross-theme interaction.

Since RANK(net cash) ≈ 1 − RANK(net debt), this expression is mechanically the profitability z-score *minus* the already-archived NetDebtWeightedOperatingProfit, so it is a sign-flipped decomposition of a tested signal whose result is largely predictable as an RMW tilt plus the negated prior alpha rather than a substantively new mechanism.

The runway framing is coherent and the coverage fix over the archived coverage ratio is a real improvement, but adding a stock (che) to a flow (oibdp) means cash-rich firms will dominate the numerator, so the signal risks collapsing into the well-known cash-holdings/liquidity ratio and should be diagnosed against a cash/lct-only benchmark.

This is an unweighted difference of two separately published anomalies — gross profitability/assets (RMW) and net debt issuance (Spiess–Affleck-Graves, Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan external financing) — in incommensurate raw units, so any result is a rediscovery of known effects rather than evidence of a genuine profitability–financing interaction.

The mean-over-volatility distance-to-default structure is economically motivated and the rank aggregation sensibly handles the fat tails of oiadp/lt, though the two legs are individually close to known profitability and earnings-volatility anomalies and the 5-year VOL window will cost coverage, so incremental value over each leg alone must be demonstrated.

The MIN combiner is a genuinely different functional form that tests complementarity rather than substitutability and is a legitimate contrast to the multiplicative gate, but it shares its entire ingredient set with archived signals and, because MIN is flat whenever one leg is high, most cross-sectional variation will come from whichever leg is weaker — a dependency worth diagnosing.

Internally consistent and correctly signed, but it is a single-leg component swap on the archive's already-tested WeakestLinkProfitSolvency (identical MIN combiner, identical industry-ranked profitability leg, only the solvency leg changed from net cash/assets to cash+CFO/current liabilities), so the expected incremental information over the existing 3.56-t result is small and the two constructs will be highly correlated.

SUMRANK of two ratios sharing the same denominator (lct) is close to a monotone re-expression of the already-tested EbitdaPlusCashRunway rather than a genuine decomposition, and the cash leg is a direct restatement of the published cash-holdings/liquidity anomaly, so the "attributable profitability contribution" claim is not actually identified by this construction.

The core term Δwcap/revt is the classic working-capital accruals anomaly (Sloan 1996) in only lightly disguised form, and the short-term-debt gate reproduces the exact conditioning structure of the archive's CashConversionUnderMaturityPressure, so this is largely a known effect re-wrapped in an existing failed-slope interaction.

This is the well-documented book-tax difference anomaly (Lev-Nissim, Hanlon) in crude form, and the expression contradicts the hypothesis in two ways — txt is total tax expense including the deferred component, so it is not the "cash-verified" measure claimed (txpd would be), and pairing pre-depreciation, pre-interest EBITDA against a post-everything tax line makes the rank gap largely a proxy for capital intensity and leverage rather than unvalidated profit.

The gross-margin channel is a genuinely different economic mechanism from the aggregate ROA trend that failed in LeveredTurnaroundTrend and the expression's sign is coherent (non-negative leverage rank preserves the z-score sign), though it reuses a leverage-gating structure that has now produced weak or wrong-signed results twice in the archive, so prior odds are modest.

Adding depreciation to the obligation denominator is a substantive, economically motivated fix to the vanishing-denominator problem that forced heavy winsorization in the archive's best-slope signal, and it should raise coverage — but note the construct changes meaning across the debt distribution (for near-debt-free firms it degenerates to EBITDA/depreciation, a capital-intensity measure rather than a solvency one), which should be checked in the diagnostics.

Internally consistent and correctly signed, but it is largely a MIN-recombination of two archived objects (MaintenanceAndDebtCoverage and the cash-over-current-liabilities half of EbitdaPlusCashRunway) using the combiner already validated in WeakestLinkProfitSolvency, so the incremental economic content is modest even though the solvency-vs-liquidity distinction is defensible.

TS_MIN of the fixed-claim coverage ratio is a genuinely distinct temporal statistic (realized downside floor rather than level, trend, dispersion, or within-history rank) with a clean stress-test interpretation and a correctly signed hypothesis; the main risk is that a five-year minimum is so persistent and so highly correlated with the contemporaneous level that it adds little beyond the archived MaintenanceAndDebtCoverage.

This is a numerator swap within an already heavily populated archive family (OperatingCoverageOfObligations, AfterTaxProfitToLiabilities, oiadp/lt inside EarningsDistanceToDefault) and mechanically decomposes into published gross profitability times the inverse of book leverage, so it is a cosmetic variant of known anomalies rather than a new mechanism.

The proposal explicitly states it changes only the combiner on DistressFinancingWithoutProfits, which is precisely the cosmetic-variant path the objective warns against, and the resulting MIN(profitability rank, negative debt-growth rank) is structurally near-identical to the archived WeakestLinkProfitSolvency while its two legs are separately well-known anomalies (profitability and debt issuance/asset growth).

The substitutes-vs-complements question is a legitimate and untested functional-form hypothesis and the liquidation-coverage leg (act/lt) is new to the archive, but MIN and MAX of two ranks are both dominated by the common component of the two ranks, so the test discriminates the two economic stories only weakly and a positive result may simply restate an additive composite.

This is a rank-and-industry-normalize transform of the archived EbitdaPlusCashRunway rather than a substantively different construct, and the stated diagnosis is partly wrong because the archived version was already winsorized at 1%, so extreme right-tail contamination cannot be the full explanation of the slope-alpha gap.

This is a mechanical leg-addition to the archive's winning MIN construct whose profitability leg was already tested in WeakestLinkProfitSolvency, and the three-way minimum of ranks predictably concentrates on whichever leg is noisiest, so it offers an attribution footnote rather than a new mechanism and its hypothesis ("the market prices the average") is not identified by the expression.

By its own admission this is a smoothing robustness check on the archive leader with legs and combiner held fixed, and the persistence dimension was already probed by StressTestedFixedClaimCoverage's five-year TS_MIN, making it the cosmetic-variant case the objective explicitly warns against.

The level-plus-direction complementarity is a genuinely new combiner for this archive, but deflating liabilities by gross profit without a positivity screen makes lt/(revt−cogs) flip sign for negative-gross-profit firms, so NEG() assigns the worst-off firms top "low burden" ranks — an internal inconsistency with the hypothesis that also contaminates the DELTA leg.

Because xint/lt is small and highly persistent, this is dominated by ΔROA — the well-documented profitability-change/earnings-momentum predictor — and the hypothesis about *crossing* the zero-spread boundary is not what a continuous first difference computes.

The expression is just EBITDA-to-assets plus negative-net-debt-to-assets with arbitrary unit weights, i.e. an unweighted sum of two separately published anomalies (profitability, cash/leverage) and a close cousin of the archive's EbitdaPlusCashRunway, so it tests linearity at the cost of proposing no new economics.

Substituting working-capital-over-liabilities for cash-over-current-liabilities keeps the economic role of the liquidity leg while stripping out the published cash-holdings content, making this a well-posed and cheap attribution test that changes the signal's information content rather than merely its parameterization.

This is a single-operator relabeling (RANK→IND_RANK) of the archived SolvencyWithWorkingCapitalSlack rather than new economic content, and industry-neutralizing distress ranks is both a standard construction choice and mechanically close to a cosmetic variant of the pair's best existing signal.

The two-dimensional realized stress test is a genuinely distinct object rather than a smoothing of either archived leg, but stacking TS_MIN inside MIN doubles the exposure to a single idiosyncratic bad year, compresses cross-sectional variation, and will further thin an already ~12% coverage sample, so the informational payoff is uncertain.

Holding the combiner and coverage leg fixed while swapping the liquidity leg for a cumulative self-financing cushion is a clean attribution experiment with a real economic distinction (stock of past earnings vs. stock of liquid resources), though re/lt is close to an Altman Z component and the result will need to be read against that known ingredient.

The expected sign is reverse-engineered from one archived signal's unexplained positive alpha despite its negative (insignificant) FMB slope and despite the well-documented negative return premium on distress/leverage, so the hypothesis is post-hoc rather than prior-driven, and the construct itself (operating leverage + financial leverage rank sum) is close to published leverage/cost-rigidity anomalies.

Testing substitutability in dollar space against the MIN combiner's complementarity claim is a legitimate and informative contrast, but the numerator sums a one-year flow (oibdp) with a balance-sheet stock (wcap) against a mixed flow/stock denominator, so the ratio has no clean units and its scale is likely to be dominated by working-capital-heavy sectors.

Averaging two highly correlated liquidity cuts is a modest, largely mechanical blend of two archived components, but the rank transform is a defensible fix for EbitdaPlusCashRunway's flow-vs-alpha disagreement (fmb 0.35 against ls_talpha 4.32), which gives the test a specific diagnostic purpose rather than being pure recombination.

A legitimate cross-family pairing of the archive's best slope leg (gross margin) with its best alpha leg (wcap/lt) using the MIN combiner that has repeatedly worked here, with no shared variables and a coherent complementarity story, though it remains an incremental leg swap within an already well-mined family.

Netting cash out of the load leg is economically defensible and materially reorders cash-rich levered firms rather than rescaling them, but it is a modest refinement of the archived leader whose incremental information over gross liabilities is likely small since che is typically a minor fraction of lt.

The financial-versus-operating-claims decomposition is the single most defensible remaining variation on the leader's load leg and yields an interpretable three-way comparison, but like Signal 2 it is a one-variable substitution within an already-tested construct rather than a new mechanism.

The ingredients (earnings-stream volatility × leverage) replicate the economics of the archived CashFlowVolatilityLeverageDefaultProxy and sit close to the published earnings-volatility/distress-risk anomalies, so only the combiner and the scaling denominator are genuinely new; the change is more than cosmetic but the incremental hypothesis content is thin.

The expression algebraically reduces to gross margin minus lt/revt, and since gross margin is bounded in [0,1] while lt/revt is unbounded and far more dispersed, the composite is dominated by the leverage-to-sales leg — so it does not test the claimed "balanced pooling" and largely reduces to a single known leverage ratio.

The construct is internally inconsistent with its negative expected sign: MIN(RANK(margin), RANK(load)) is monotonically increasing in gross margin, a leg the archive shows predicts returns positively, and its low tail pools genuinely safe low-load firms with genuinely weak low-margin firms, so both tails are muddled and the direction is unidentified — the same defect that produced ProfitableButIlliquid's wrong-signed slope.

With MIN, MAX, SUB and (via SUMRANK elsewhere) additive combinations of exactly these two legs already in the archive, the product of the same two ranks is a fourth combiner on an unchanged information set — a cosmetic functional-form permutation whose result will be nearly indistinguishable from the additive rank composite it approximates monotonically.

Because lt already contains dltt and dlc, this is an arbitrary 2x re-weighting of a component inside an existing denominator, and the resulting load rank will be very highly correlated with both archived variants, so it cannot cleanly test the stated enforceability mechanism.

This is a legitimate and cleanly designed ablation isolating whether the revenue denominator or the claim stack drives the leading construct, though its two legs (gross margin, book leverage) are both individually well-known and the expected outcome is informative-but-weaker rather than a new alpha source.

Pairing the archive's two strongest but differently-normalized legs (profit-flow coverage vs. sales-scaled claim load) is coherent and untried, but it is the Nth MIN-of-two-ranks in a saturated family and the legs share the debt stock, so incremental information over the existing leaders may be modest.

Transferring the demonstrated-resilience (worst-realized-state) concept to the per-sales family is economically motivated, internally consistent in sign (TS_MIN on margin, NEG TS_MAX on load), and tests a genuinely different object — proven downside capacity rather than current level — with only a modest survivorship/coverage caveat from the five-year window.

Substituting a cash-flow claim (interest per sales dollar, which embeds the lender-assessed credit spread) for the stock-based load legs is a substantively different mechanism rather than a rescaling, but the signal risks degenerating into a debt-free indicator given the large mass of firms with near-zero xint, and interest coverage itself is close to standard credit-screen territory.

This is a mechanical operator swap (TS_MIN/TS_MAX → MA) on the archive's StressTestedUnitEconomics with identical inputs, window, and structure, and since five-year averages and five-year minima of margin and load are highly rank-correlated it is likely to produce a near-duplicate result with little attribution power.

The economic point that a historical claim-load maximum is stale while a margin floor reveals durable unit economics is legitimate, but the construct is a one-leg ablation sitting strictly between two already-tested signals (MarginAndObligationLoadPerSale and StressTestedUnitEconomics) and so is a cosmetic interpolation rather than a substantively new mechanism.

Placing the stress test in the scale denominator is a genuinely different construct from the archive's historical-load-maximum version, but the reviewer should note that lt/TS_MIN(revt) mechanically embeds negative five-year sales growth, so the signal risks being a partial repackaging of the well-known sales/asset-growth anomaly rather than a distress measure.

The near-term cash-service framing is economically sound, but the archive already tested MarginAfterAnnualDebtService using exactly the same variables — gross margin, xint+dlc, and revenue — so this is primarily a functional-form change (subtraction → weakest-link MIN) on an established construct rather than new information.

Industry-demeaning the gross-margin leg is the one untested conditioning choice on the family's alpha-generating component, it is economically well-motivated (margin levels are technology-determined), it materially reorders the long leg rather than rescaling it, and it costs nothing in coverage.

Testing EBITDA margin against gross margin in the leading per-sales pairing is a clean, high-coverage examination of an assumption the archive never validated, though it is a single-input substitution with limited upside and its outcome will be hard to interpret if the two margin measures rank most firms similarly.

This is mechanical stacking of three already-tested legs into a triple MIN, which by construction collapses onto the weakest rank (compressing dispersion and creating ties) and will be highly correlated with the existing IndustryRelativeMarginLoad and MaturityConcentrationWithMargin signals without introducing any new economic content.

The construct is internally coherent and economically sensible, but it is a single-operator industry-demeaning swap applied to the already-archived MaturityConcentrationWithMargin — exactly the RANK→IND_RANK re-parameterization already tested on the load pairing — so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different mechanism.

The proxy is internally inconsistent with its own hypothesis: wcap includes cash (and short-term debt), so EBITDA that successfully converts to cash raises Δwcap and is mechanically netted back out, penalizing exactly the cash-generative firms the signal claims to identify — non-cash working capital (act − che − (lct − dlc)) would be required.

The two legs share the same gross-profit numerator and are therefore substantially redundant rather than "non-redundant," and the stated motivation mislabels TS_MIN(gross profit)/lt as a scale-sensitive dollar level when it is already a scale-free coverage ratio, so the claimed slope-to-alpha repair mechanism is not what the expression implements.

Combining industry conditioning with the within-firm margin floor addresses two genuinely distinct problems (sector composition versus downside durability) and has not been tested jointly, though the family is saturated enough that double-conditioning the margin leg risks shrinking usable dispersion and delivering only marginal incremental information.

Dropping the obligation-size leg entirely makes this the most diagnostically informative of the six — a strong result would isolate durability-plus-timing as the mechanism — though the dlc/lt leg is a mix ratio that mechanically rewards heavily long-term-levered firms and is noisy for firms with small total liabilities.
